title: Q4 AI Platform Architecture & Product Strategy Kickoff

chapters.title: Action Items, QA Strategy & Q4 Timeline

summaries.general: The engineering and product leadership aligned on Q4 goals: scaling Fathom to 50,000 monthly meetings, achieving sub-300ms transcription latency, and introducing template-based AI summaries. Alex & Marcus detailed the event-driven Redis pub/sub receiver architecture. Elena presented the split-screen user interface with real-time highlights and virtualized transcript playback.
summaries.sales: Target Commercial Outcome: Sub-300ms transcription latency positioning enables Fathom to secure Enterprise SLAs. Estimated infrastructure cost savings of 38% via TensorRT FP16 model optimizations on T4 GPUs.
summaries.oneOnOne: Sarah Jenkins aligned with Rachel Adams on ownership of the 6-week release timeline and cross-functional team milestones.
summaries.standup: Identified core bottleneck in worker pod memory starvation during peak volume. Decoupled WebRTC receiver from speech inference via Redis buffer. LocalStorage state persistence added to prevent highlight data loss.
actionItems: Alex Rivera: Publish technical RFC for tokenized WebSocket streaming protocol by Friday.
Elena Rostova: Export high-fidelity Figma icons and participant badges by Wednesday.
Marcus Chen & David Kim: Finalize local storage persistence fallback and virtual list scrolling.
James Wilson: Provision staging Kubernetes clusters with GPU autoscaling.
Maya Patel: Build Playwright automated test suite for multi-speaker overlap scenarios.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Good morning everyone. Welcome to the Q4 AI Platform Strategy and Architecture kickoff.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Excited to be here, Sarah. We have ambitious goals for this quarter, especially around scale and latency.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Our primary target for Q4 is doubling our concurrent meeting capacity while cutting transcription latency to under 300ms.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: That latency target is aggressive, but with our new streaming pipeline proposal, it's definitely within reach.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: From the core backend perspective, our bottleneck has been payload deserialization during peak volume spikes.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: And on the UI side, users have requested faster visual updates when highlights are created in real time.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: Right now the state hydration causes a slight UI flicker when multiple participants bookmark simultaneously.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: DevOps is ready to support the new node clusters. We've benchmarked auto-scaling groups on AWS.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: We need to ensure regression suites cover multi-speaker audio overlap tests before we deploy to staging.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Great call Maya. Quality can't take a back seat to speed. Rachel, can you review the product roadmap highlights?

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Phase 1 focuses on real-time transcript streaming. Phase 2 introduces template-based smart summaries.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Phase 3 will add localized storage persistence for off-line editing and instant highlight sharing.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Phase 3 aligns nicely with our effort to reduce database round-trips for non-critical transient user notes.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: We've also redesigned the sidebar layout to make switching between Sales, Standup, and 1:1 templates instantaneous.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: I've already tested pre-rendering those templates on the client, and load times are under 50ms.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Outstanding. Let's dive deep into the architectural challenges we need Alex and Marcus to address.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: We should also look at how WebSockets handle reconnects during transient mobile network drops.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: I propose an exponential backoff retry mechanism with local event queue buffering.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: If local storage buffers un-sent highlights, the user won't even notice a temporary network loss.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: We can display a subtle inline status chip saying 'Syncing locally...' during reconnects.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: That reduces support tickets significantly during ISP hiccups.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: QA can simulate network throttling in Playwright to verify packet retransmission.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Let's make sure the reconnect timeout is set to 30 seconds before declaring a disconnected state.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Agreed. Now let's dive into Chapter 2: System Architecture & Bottlenecks.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Thanks Sarah. Looking at telemetry from last week, we processed 14,000 active audio channels.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: The primary bottleneck was worker pod starvation in our central ingestion service during 8+ participant rooms.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Maintaining synchronous WebSocket connections on a single monolith instance caused memory to balloon.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: Node CPU utilization hit 92% twice last Tuesday. Headroom was razor thin.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: We saw packet drops in 3% of incoming WebRTC streams, which led to dropped words in transcripts.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: That feedback came up in two enterprise customer syncs last week. Accuracy is paramount.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: What is our proposed fix for packet loss and stream fragmentation?

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: We're decoupling the WebRTC media receiver from speech-to-text inference using an event-driven Redis pub/sub buffer.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: This lets us buffer audio chunks locally in memory for up to 12 seconds without losing sync if a pod recycles.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: How does that impact client WebSocket frame rates? Will the frontend receive chunks in smaller bursts?

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Instead of sending 5-second audio blocks, we'll stream 250ms token deltas. Transcripts will render word-by-word.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: That's fantastic for user experience! It will feel like watching live closed captions on TV.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: Will word confidence scores be attached to each token delta or calculated at sentence end?

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Token deltas carry lightweight confidence weights. Sentence boundaries trigger full recalibration.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: From an infrastructure standpoint, the Redis pub/sub layer adds minimal latency—under 4ms overhead.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Sounds like a solid foundation. Marcus, how are we scaling memory allocations across regional clusters?

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: We are configuring cgroups limits so pod auto-scaling triggers at 70% memory threshold instead of 85%.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: That gives us a 90-second buffer for new Kubernetes pods to spin up and pass health checks.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: Will client connections auto-migrate seamlessly if a regional cluster degrades?

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Yes, AWS Global Accelerator will route client traffic to the nearest healthy edge node within 5 seconds.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: This high-availability setup will be a major selling point for our Enterprise sales team.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: We should add a connection health indicator icon in the top navigation bar of the app.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: QA will log chaos engineering test scenarios to validate edge node failovers under heavy load.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Excellent plan. Now let's move to Chapter 3: AI Agent & Prompt Engineering.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: For the AI summarization pipeline, we are expanding beyond generic summaries into domain-tailored templates.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: We now have specialized prompt templates for Sales Demos, 1:1 Manager Syncs, and Engineering Standups.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: Each template highlights different metrics. For Sales, it extracts objections and next steps. For Standups, blockers.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Under the hood, we are orchestrating these summaries asynchronously using background queue workers.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: Can the user customize prompt parameters on the fly, or are templates pre-compiled?

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Users will have preset defaults, but enterprise admins can inject custom instructions into prompt payloads.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: We've benchmarked inference runtime: GPT-4o mini handles chapter generation in under 1.8 seconds per meeting.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: Have we tested summary accuracy when speakers talk over each other during debate segments?

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Speaker diarization cleans up overlapping speech before passing formatted context to the LLM.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: What happens if a meeting runs over 60 minutes, like this one? How do we handle token window limits?

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: We chunk the transcript by chapters. Each chapter gets summarized independently, then a meta-summary combines them.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: That map-reduce approach works really cleanly on frontend UI too. We can render chapter cards progressively.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: Users can click on any chapter card to jump straight to that timestamp in transcript and video player.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: We should cache generated summary JSON blobs on CDN edge nodes to speed up initial page views.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Agreed. CDN caching will make shared meeting links load instantly for guest view participants.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Let's make sure guest views respect organization permission boundaries and security policies.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: Security team requested tokenized access links with configurable expiration times for external shares.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: We can generate signed URLs for meeting assets valid for 24 hours by default.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: That handles security cleanly without adding friction for authenticated workspace members.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: Can guests make highlights or are they read-only?

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Guests can view highlights but need an account to create persistent highlights.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: We'll show a friendly signup CTA modal if a guest clicks the highlight button.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: Signed URLs will also reduce bot scraping on publicly shared transcripts.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: We'll include rate-limiting test cases for signed URL generation.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Great addition. Let's discuss action item extraction accuracy.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Action items are parsed with assignee tags and due dates extracted automatically.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: We format them as structured JSON so integrations like Jira or Linear can ingest them directly.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: On the UI, action items render as checkable task lists that sync state to localStorage.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: Users can click a checkmark to mark an action item as completed right inside Fathom.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: That turns Fathom from a passive recorder into an active workflow productivity tool.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: I love that positioning. Now let's move to Chapter 4: Frontend UX Specs.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: Let me share my screen to show updated design mockups for the Fathom meeting player interface.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: Notice the split-screen view: transcript on the left, synchronized summary & highlights panel on the right.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: The visual hierarchy is super clean. Hover states on transcript lines highlight corresponding scrubber timestamps.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: We also added keyboard shortcuts: pressing 'H' creates an instant highlight at the current playback timestamp.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Keyboard shortcuts are huge for power users who want to take quick notes during live meetings.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: When pressing 'H', we immediately append the highlight object to localStorage so it feels instantaneous.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: And background sync pushes local highlights to the server when network connectivity is stable.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: What happens if two participants add a highlight at the exact same second?

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: We deduplicate highlights based on user ID and timestamp thresholds within a 2-second window.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: We've also designed color-coded highlight tags: Red for Action Item, Yellow for Key Insight, Green for Sales Win.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: Can users filter transcript lines by highlight tag color? That would be great for QA audit trails.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: Yes! The filter tab at top of transcript allows filtering by tag type or participant name.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: Rendering 500+ transcript items in DOM can get heavy. Are we using virtualized lists?

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: Yes, we're using virtual list scrolling so only visible transcript lines are present in the DOM tree.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: That keeps memory footprint under 45MB even for long 2-hour executive syncs.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Can we test this with seed data across mobile web viewports as well?

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: The mobile layout stacks video player on top and switches between Transcript and Summary tabs smoothly.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: What typography and font family are we using for high readability?

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: We chose Inter and Outfit from Google Fonts with crisp line height and high contrast dark modes.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: Tailwind CSS typography plugin makes styling long summary markdown effortless.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: We should ensure copy-to-clipboard buttons for summary snippets work natively across all browsers.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: I'll test clipboard API permissions on Safari iOS and Chrome Desktop.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: Also verify audio waveform visualizer animations don't trigger high CPU usage on low-end laptops.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: Waveforms use hardware-accelerated Canvas 2D render loops capped at 30 FPS.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: That preserves battery life for users attending back-to-back video calls on laptops.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Thoughtful UX detail Alex. Now let's jump into Chapter 5: Infrastructure & Costs.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: Let's review infrastructure projections for Q4. GPU instances for Whisper AI model inference are our largest expense.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: By switching to TensorRT-optimized fp16 models on NVIDIA T4 instances, we cut GPU costs by 38% per audio hour.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: That is a huge saving. Plus, TensorRT batch inference increases throughput from 12 streams per GPU to 28 streams.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: We've also implemented silence suppression on client mic feeds so muted participants don't consume inference cycles.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: What is our overall estimated monthly infrastructure budget with these optimizations?

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: We project staying under $18,000/month while serving up to 50,000 active monthly meetings.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: That fits comfortably inside our gross margin targets for the enterprise tier.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: Have we tested cluster failover if an AWS region experiences a transient outage?

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: We have secondary fallback routing to US-East-2 with automated DNS failover taking under 15 seconds.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: On frontend side, CDN asset delivery is configured with stale-while-revalidate headers for instant cached loads.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Latency benchmarks across 100 test runs showed 95th percentile transcription latency of 240ms. Target achieved!

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Tremendous milestone Alex. Congratulations to the core architecture team.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Thanks Sarah. It was a true cross-functional engineering effort.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: We also set up cloud cost monitoring alerts in Slack if daily spend strays by more than 10%.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Financial transparency helps us make quick product trade-offs during sprint cycles.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: Are video thumbnails stored on S3 with WebP compression?

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: Yes, WebP thumbnails average only 18KB each, loading in milliseconds.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: QA verified video player buffering works smoothly on 4G cellular connections.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Adaptive HLS streaming dynamically steps down video resolution if bandwidth drops.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Excellent resilience engineering. Let's move to Chapter 6: Action Items & Next Steps.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Let's wrap up by assigning clear action items and agreeing on sprint milestones for next 6 weeks.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Sprint 1 starts Monday: focus on API data models, seed data verification, and localStorage highlight hook scaffolding.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: I'll take ownership of building responsive Next.js layout, header navigation, and theme system.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: I'll provide full Figma asset exports for meeting control icons, tag badges, and custom participant avatars.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: I'll finalize JSON seed schema and write local mock service worker for faked bot audio playback.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: I'll publish technical RFC for tokenized WebSocket streaming protocol by end of day Friday.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: DevOps will set up preview deployment pipelines on Vercel with automatic pull request builds.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: QA will draft automated Playwright test scripts covering meeting search, filtering, and local highlight persistence.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Can we ensure our seed datasets include realistic meetings across various lengths and templates?

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Yes, we'll seed 10 distinct meetings: from quick 15-minute standups to this 60-minute multi-participant kickoff.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: We'll also test edge cases like long transcripts with over 150 speech lines to verify virtual list performance.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: Sounds great! The UI will render thousands of lines smoothly without any layout lag.

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: Really excited to see complete application come together over coming sprints.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Marcus, can you verify seed meeting data contains rich summaries across all template types?

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Yes, each seed meeting contains General, Sales, 1:1, Standup, and Action Items sections.

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: And we've added realistic avatars, roles, and timestamps to make the demo feel totally alive.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: Vercel deployment setup will allow instant previews for every git commit.

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: I'll perform full cross-browser testing on Chrome, Safari, and Firefox before tagging production v1.0.

transcript.speaker: David Kim
transcript.text: I'll also ensure mobile responsive navigation works cleanly on mobile Safari.

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Architecture docs will be updated in project wiki for future onboardings.

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Does anyone have any final questions before we adjourn?

transcript.speaker: Elena Rostova
transcript.text: All clear on design specs!

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: Backend ready for Sprint 1!

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: DevOps ready for Vercel deploy!

transcript.speaker: Maya Patel
transcript.text: QA ready with test suites!

transcript.speaker: Sarah Jenkins
transcript.text: Thank you everyone for great discussion and crisp execution plan. Let's crush Q4!

transcript.speaker: Rachel Adams
transcript.text: Thanks all, see you in sprint planning!

transcript.speaker: Alex Rivera
transcript.text: Bye everyone, great meeting!

title: Post-Mortem Review - API Latency Spike Incident #408

chapters.title: Root Cause Analysis: Redis Connection Pool Exhaustion

summaries.general: Blameless post-mortem review of Incident #408. Root cause was Redis connection pool exhaustion during a 300% traffic surge. Implemented connection pooling and circuit breaker protection.
actionItems: James Wilson: Upgrade Redis cluster instance size and tune maxconnections setting.
Marcus Chen: Implement resilience4j circuit breaker around audio worker calls.

transcript.speaker: James Wilson
transcript.text: Let me begin the blameless post-mortem for Incident #408. Latency spiked to 4.2s at 14:15 UTC yesterday.

transcript.speaker: Marcus Chen
transcript.text: The root cause was Redis connection pool exhaustion when 50 worker pods simultaneously reconnected after a network blip.
